newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus deputies seek to impeach president.
newsitem.headline: Belarus deputies seek to impeach president.

text.p: Members of parliament in Belarus said on Monday they had started impeachment moves against President Alexander Lukashenko, who they have branded a dictator.

Lukashenko also faced a mutiny in his usually loyal government. Prime Minister Mikhail Chigir said he would resign unless Lukashenko cancelled a referendum, set for Sunday, that would boost his powers in the former Soviet republic.
"Parliament has gathered enough deputies' signatures, more than 70, to start the impeachment process," liberal deputy Alexander Dobravolski said.
But Lukashenko's top aide, Vladimir Zametalin, told Reuters the 42-year-old president could stop parliament impeaching him even if the constitutional court approved such a decision.
"The president of the republic will use the maximum possibilities available to him to get out of the situation without conflict," Zametalin said in a telephone interview.
Asked if this could include dissolving parliament and the constitutional court, he said: "It's entirely possible. The president has many options."

The start of impeachment moves stepped up a battle between Lukashenko and parliament over the president's efforts to change the constitution to introduce presidential rule in the country of 10 million.

If the constitutional court approved the deputies' impeachment moves, 132 members of parliament would have to vote in favour of the decision. Only 108 deputies, including some who back Lukashenko, attended Monday's session.
The parliament was due to meet again on Tuesday and invited the president to attend the session.

Chigir's resignation threat was another blow to Lukashenko. The prime minister has in the past been loyal to him and Zametalin said the president had not made a decision yet about whether to accept the resignation.
Lukashenko hit back at a rally in the southern city of Gomel, telling his opponents they should be ready to flee Belarus if he wins the referendum, which would extend his term by more than two years.
"From November 25 we will put things straight and everyone will have to work," Lukashanko told a rally in the country's second largest city.
"Whoever doesn't want this will have to find another motherland...I am not trying to scare anyone but that's how it will be."

In Paris, members of the North Atlantic Assembly, which groups parliamentarians from 40 European and North American countries including the 16 NATO states, voiced strong support for the Belarus parliament against Lukashenko.
Assembly president Karsten Voigt of Germany told a news conference that Lukashenko's behaviour was "illegal, non-democratic and sometimes even crazy".
About 1,000 anti-Lukashenko demonstrators kept up a vigil outside parliament late on Monday, cheering speeches which were relayed by loudspeaker to Independence Square.
Dozens of police guarded the entrances to the building in the shadow of a huge statue to Soviet founder Vladimir Lenin.
"I fear it will end in street battles," said Natalya, 42, a librarian waiting for a trolleybus.
Lukashenko has infuriated nationalists with derisory comments on the Belarussian language and his desire to form a union with neighbouring Russia.

He keeps a tight rein on the press and state-run television runs daily advertisements urging people to take advantage of early voting before Sunday's referendum, when voters face a baffling list of questions posed by president and parliament.
